findings.quote: We propose to issue an unqualified opinion on the Council's financial statements as soon as practically possible following the Audit Committee on 23 September 2026.

findings.paper_title: 10z External Audit Annual Audit Report Appendix 1
findings.headline: Capital programme continues to slip, with £19.4m (20%) of approved budget not spent in 2025/26.
findings.detail: Capital expenditure was £77.526m (80%) against a budget of £97.267m, with the £19.440m underspend attributed to project slippage into future years. The auditor notes that moderate levels of slippage continue to be reported, though performance improved slightly during 2025/26 compared with the previous year. The capital programme is subject to regular monitoring with clear approval and prioritisation processes.
findings.matters: Ongoing capital slippage of 20% indicates project delivery risks and may suggest that planned capital works, potentially including income-generating or efficiency-enabling schemes, are being delayed, affecting service improvement.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure £77.526m against budget £97.267m; underspend £19.440m (20% of budget).
findings.quote: Capital expenditure was £77.526m (80%) against a budget of £97.267m, with a £19.440m underspend largely due to project slippage into future years.

findings.paper_title: 10z External Audit Annual Audit Report Appendix 1
findings.headline: Council reported a £2.6m revenue overspend in 2025/26, funded from reserves.
findings.detail: The Council spent £2.631m more than budgeted in 2025/26 revenue expenditure, which was funded from General Fund reserves. General Fund reserves increased slightly from £91.781m to £92.381m despite the overspend. The Council has set a balanced revenue budget for 2026/27 including £7.24m of savings and a 4.99% council tax increase including 2% adult social care precept.
findings.matters: While the overspend was modest and absorbed by reserves, it indicates ongoing budget control challenges and reliance on reserves to manage year-end positions, particularly concerning given the DSG deficit is already consuming 50% of those reserves.
findings.figures: Revenue overspend £2.631m (2025/26); General Fund reserves £92.381m (2025/26) vs £91.781m (2024/25); 2026/27 council tax increase 4.99%.
findings.quote: In 2025/26, the Council reported a small revenue overspend of £2.631m, funded from reserves. General Fund reserves increased from £91.8m to £92.4m.

findings.paper_title: 10z External Audit Annual Audit Report Appendix 1
findings.headline: Transformation governance plan remains incomplete three years after initial recommendation.
findings.detail: A 2023/24 recommendation that the Council identify and document all transformation activities within one plan remains outstanding, with the auditor retaining it as an improvement recommendation in 2025/26. A draft transformation plan is expected to be taken to scrutiny panels in October 2026 ahead of adoption at Cabinet in November. Until a single consolidated plan is in place, the Council may lack effective oversight of transformation activity and corresponding savings opportunities.
findings.matters: Non-implementation of a three-year-old governance recommendation suggests either weak implementation capacity or insufficient priority, increasing the risk that planned savings are not delivered in full or on time.
findings.figures: Recommendation first raised 2023/24; draft plan expected October 2026, adoption November 2026.
findings.quote: this recommendation remains outstanding although progress is being made, with a draft transformation plan expected to be taken to Scrutiny panels in October ahead of adoption at Cabinet alongside the MTFS in November.

findings.paper_title: 10z External Audit Annual Audit Report Appendix 1
findings.headline: Savings delivery rate fell from 77% to 65%, with only 65% of the £14m target delivered in full.
findings.detail: The Council's full savings delivery rate declined to 65% (£9.149m of £14.012m target) compared with 77% in 2024/25. A further 15% was mitigated by other means and 20% was delayed into 2026/27, indicating increasing reliance on non-direct solutions. The auditor notes that overall the Council has adequate savings plans and identifies achievable savings, but the trajectory has slipped, and the Council has a new savings target of £7.24m for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Declining savings delivery rate suggests the Council's ability to manage its budget position is deteriorating, increasing the risk that future budget gaps cannot be closed and may require further reserve drawdowns or borrowing.
findings.figures: 2025/26 savings target £14.012m, delivered in full 65% (£9.149m), mitigated 15% (£2.040m), delayed 20% (£2.823m); 2024/25 full delivery rate 77%; 2026/27 savings target £7.24m.
findings.quote: £9.149m (65%) was delivered in full (compared to 77% in 2024/25), a further 15% (£2.040m) was mitigated by other means, and the remaining 20% (£2.823m) was delayed until 2026/27 or addressed through the budget setting proposals.

findings.paper_title: 10z External Audit Annual Audit Report Appendix 1
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit grew by £13.7m (41.8%) to £46.5m, equivalent to 50% of usable reserves.
findings.detail: The DSG deficit increased by £13.7m to £46.5m during 2025/26, a significant weakness identified in both 2024/25 and retained in 2025/26. The Council has submitted a SEND Reform Plan seeking High Needs Sustainability Grant funding expected to cover 90% of this deficit, though approval is pending, and recovery plans estimate further unmitigated deficits of £17.2m in 2026/27 and £18.8m in 2027/28. If not resolved by the 31 March 2028 override deadline, these accumulating deficits will need to be funded from the Council's own reserves.
findings.matters: A £46.5m liability growing at 41.8% annually, dependent on uncertain government grant approval and unresolved underlying SEND demand, poses a material risk to the Council's medium-term financial sustainability and reserve levels.
findings.figures: Deficit £46.513m (2025/26), increase of £13.717m (41.8%), equivalent to approximately 50% of usable reserves; forecast further deficits £17.2m (2026/27) and £18.8m (2027/28); HNSG expected to cover 90%.
findings.quote: The deficit increased by £13.717m (41.8%) during 2025/26 to £46.513m, equivalent to around 50% of usable reserves, indicating that current actions have not yet reduced the underlying cause of the deficit, as evidenced by the increase.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statement of Accounts 202526 Appendix 3
findings.headline: Bath Quays South project has experienced delays in achieving rental income and in implementing corporate landlord savings, creating a £0.665m pressure in 2025/26 funded from the Commercial Income Risk Reserve.
findings.detail: Capital regeneration schemes, particularly Bath Quays South, have faced delays in leasing floor space and delays in implementing planned corporate landlord model efficiencies. This created a £1.593m overall adverse variance in the Corporate Estate and Regeneration area, of which £0.665m relates specifically to Bath Quays South. The pressure was proposed to be funded from the Commercial Income Risk Reserve. Delays in both capital projects and their expected commercial returns suggest execution risk in major development initiatives.
findings.matters: A lender should be concerned if major capital projects are slipping and failing to generate expected commercial returns on time, as this indicates project delivery risk and optimistic assumptions in the capital plan.
findings.figures: £0.665m Bath Quays South pressure; £1.593m overall adverse variance in Corporate Estate and Regeneration
findings.quote: Delays in renting floor space at No.1 Bath Quays South, and delays implementing the corporate landlord model and rationalising the estate were the remaining contributors to the adverse year-end position resulting in a £1.593m adverse variance across Corporate Estate and Regeneration.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statement of Accounts 202526 Appendix 3
findings.headline: Heritage Services income target was significantly missed in 2025/26 due to lower-than-budgeted visitor numbers, particularly in peak pricing periods, creating a £2.454m adverse variance.
findings.detail: The council set an 'aggressive' income target for Heritage Services for 2025/26. Visitor numbers fell materially short of budget, with larger shortfalls occurring specifically during peak pricing months, limiting revenue offset. One-off restructuring costs, which the council says will yield savings in 2026/27, also contributed to the adverse position. The variance is material and suggests income targets may be optimistic or that the heritage offer is underperforming.
findings.matters: A lender should be concerned if the council is setting income targets aggressively and then missing them significantly, as this suggests either budget realism issues or strategic underperformance in commercial services.
findings.figures: £2.454m adverse variance in Heritage Services within Economic & Cultural Sustainable Development portfolio
findings.quote: An aggressive income target was set for Heritage Services for 2025/26, but unfortunately visitor numbers were lower than budgeted, with larger visitor shortfalls crucially happening during months with peak pricing periods.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statement of Accounts 202526 Appendix 3
findings.headline: The council's Core Spending Power is growing by only 8.4% over 2026/27–2028/29, well below the England average of 15.5%, and the council is the 4th lowest funded unitary authority in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The government's Fair Funding reforms reduced B&NES funding. The council initially forecast a £13.00m negative impact over three years; the actual announced impact was £12.55m (£0.45m better). Even with this improvement, CSP growth is only 8.4% over the three-year period versus the England average of 15.5%. A published comparison in the paper places Bath & North East Somerset as the 4th lowest funded unitary authority in 2026/27 by CSP per head of population, indicating structural funding constraint.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's structural deficits are demand-driven or funding-driven. Low funding relative to peers, combined with high-demand services like social care, indicates systemic financial stress beyond the council's control.
findings.figures: 8.4% cumulative CSP growth 2026/27–2028/29; England average 15.5%; Fair Funding negative impact £12.55m over 3 years; 4th lowest funded unitary authority 2026/27
findings.quote: For England, CSP for local government is increasing by 15.5% across the three year period covering 2026/27 to 2028/29. For the Council, the CSP is shown to increase by 8.4%, well below the England average and reflecting the negative impact of the Fair Funding changes.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statement of Accounts 202526 Appendix 3
findings.headline: The council covered its £2.631m general fund overspend by drawing down reserves (£1.176m from Commercial Risk Reserve and £1.455m from Corporate Revenue Budget Contingency), reducing financial resilience.
findings.detail: Total net spending was £171.163m against a revised budget of £168.635m. The resulting year-end overspend of £2.631m was funded by the Cabinet approving transfers from earmarked reserves rather than rebalancing budgets. The uncommitted General Fund balance (unearmarked reserves) remains at £12.584m, which the council confirms is within the risk-assessed target range, but the pattern of using reserves to cover recurring overspends indicates structural imbalance.
findings.matters: A lender should be concerned if the council is using reserves to balance the budget rather than rebalancing spending; this suggests structural imbalance and reduces the council's resilience to absorb future pressures.
findings.figures: £2.631m overspend 2025/26; £1.176m withdrawn from Commercial Risk Reserve; £1.455m withdrawn from Corporate Revenue Budget Contingency; £12.584m uncommitted General Fund balance
findings.quote: The Cabinet Outturn report includes the proposed transfer of the £1.176mm from the Commercial Risk Reserve and £1.455m from the Corporate Revenue Budget Contingency earmarked reserve to fund the overspend position.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statement of Accounts 202526 Appendix 3
findings.headline: The council released £7.22m of corporately held contingency in 2026/27 and deployed £9.830m contingency during 2025/26, leaving only £2.62m contingency cover on a £193.17m net revenue budget.
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget included £9.830m in corporate contingencies to cover savings delivery risk, contract inflation impacts and demand cost increases. All of this was released during the year to offset service pressures. For 2026/27, a further £7.22m of corporate contingency was released to fund growth pressures, leaving £2.62m contingency held within the budget. This extremely low contingency reserve (1.4% of net revenue budget) provides minimal headroom to absorb unexpected pressures.
findings.matters: A lender should be concerned by very low contingency cover in a council facing material social care demand pressures and where savings delivery is at risk; the council is operating with reduced financial resilience.
findings.figures: £9.830m contingency released in 2025/26 (100% of budgeted contingency); £7.22m released from corporate contingency for 2026/27 growth; £2.62m remaining contingency in 2026/27 budget on £193.17m net revenue budget
findings.quote: All £9.830m of budgeted contingency has been released within the outturn position to partially offset pressures across council services... This releases £7.22m of the corporately held contingency which formed part of the 2025/26 base budget. This leaves contingency held within the 2026/27 budget of £2.62m.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statement of Accounts 202526 Appendix 3
findings.headline: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit will total £46.505m by year-end, but a new government grant is expected to fund 90% of this, leaving a £4.573m residual gap from 2028/29 onwards.
findings.detail: The accumulated DSG deficit at year-end is £46.505m (brought forward £32.789m plus in-year £13.716m overspend on the High Needs Block). The council cannot fund this from its General Fund without Secretary of State permission and must hold it in an unusable reserve under statutory override through 31 March 2028. The Department for Education has announced a High Needs Stability Grant expected to pay 90% of the accumulated deficit (anticipated £41.931m) in autumn 2026, leaving a residual £4.573m gap the council will fund from 2028/29 when the statutory override ends. The DFE will take over the High Needs Block from April 2028.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's school funding crisis is council-driven or system-driven, and whether it is time-limited. The £4.573m residual gap from 2028/29 is a medium-term pressure the council will own after government support ends.
findings.figures: £46.505m total DSG deficit to carry forward; £13.716m in-year High Needs overspend; £41.931m anticipated government grant (90% of deficit); £4.573m residual gap from 2028/29
findings.quote: Once an acceptable plan has been provided to the DFE they will pay the LA a grant equal to 90% of the accumulated deficit of the DSG. It is anticipated that the Council would receive a grant of £41.931m leaving a residual gap of £4.573m to be funded by the Council from 2028/29 when the Statutory override will end.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statement of Accounts 202526 Appendix 3
findings.headline: Only 65% of the council's 2025/26 savings targets were delivered in full; 20% slipped to 2026/27, and the 'Being Our Best' programme target was entirely missed.
findings.detail: Of £14.01m in approved 2025/26 savings, 65% (£9.15m) were delivered in full, 15% (£2.04m) were mitigated through contingency or other savings, and 20% (£2.82m) were delayed or addressed through budget setting. The 'Being Our Best Programme' savings target of £2.479m was not delivered in year; a reduced target of £2.209m was carried forward to 2026/27 and allocated out to services for delivery. This pattern indicates savings delivery risk undermining the credibility of the medium-term plan.
findings.matters: A lender should be concerned if the council's savings plans show a pattern of under-delivery or slippage, as this undermines confidence in the credibility of closing the £32.92m medium-term gap.
findings.figures: £14.01m 2025/26 savings; 65% (£9.15m) delivered in full; 15% (£2.04m) mitigated; 20% (£2.82m) delayed; £2.479m 'Being Our Best' target missed; £2.209m carried to 2026/27
findings.quote: In relation to the 2025/26 approved savings of £14.01m, 65% (£9.15m) have been delivered in full, 15% (£2.04m) have been mitigated through savings, contingency or income elsewhere in the respective service, with the remaining 20% (£2.82m) delayed until 2026/27 or addressed through the budget setting proposals.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statement of Accounts 202526 Appendix 3
findings.headline: Children's Services recorded a £10.182m overspend in 2025/26, driven by residential placement costs escalating from demand and market cost inflation.
findings.detail: The service carried a £4.775m overspend from 2024/25 forward. A late-year increase of eight residential placements in Q4 2024/25 created a recurring £2.700m pressure. During 2025/26, further placements and extensions added £4.567m, with £1.510m of additional pressure arising in Q4 2025/26 alone. Of the total £8.107m residential placements overspend, £0.840m relates to invoices from 2024/25 written off as unrecoverable. The council cites market cost inflation driven by limited placement sufficiency and increasing complexity of need.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if social care demand is driving structural, uncontrollable overspends in a service the council cannot easily cut; escalating placements and invoices written off indicate deeper cost management issues.
findings.figures: £10.182m overspend; £4.775m brought forward deficit; £8.107m residential placements overspend of which £4.567m new in-year; £0.840m invoices written off
findings.quote: Despite additional budget provision in 2025/26, a late-year increase of eight residential placements in quarter 4 of 2024/25 created a recurring £2.700m budget pressure. During 2025/26, this was compounded by further additional residential placements and extensions to existing placements to meet safeguarding and care needs, increasing the residential placements overspend by a further £4.567m.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statement of Accounts 202526 Appendix 3
findings.headline: The council faces a structural budget deficit of £32.92m over the five-year period 2026/27 to 2030/31, starting with a balanced 2026/27 budget but opening to £12.59m deficit in 2027/28.
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy assumes savings and income generation of £7.24m will balance the 2026/27 budget. However, the planning table discloses deficits of £12.59m (2027/28), £10.47m (2028/29), £4.95m (2029/30) and £4.91m (2030/31). The council states the gap is expected to reduce through income growth, efficiencies and a developing transformation programme, but no credible path to closure is articulated in this paper.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can close a £32.92m deficit through actions within its control, or whether it reflects systemic funding shortfall; a £193.17m net revenue budget with a £12.59m deficit in year two suggests structural imbalance.
findings.quote: The updated plan shows a balanced budget for 2026/27 with a future years budget gap from 2027/28, although this is expected to reduce to a balanced position once further efficiencies and transformation programme are factored in.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statemenet of Account 202526 Appendix 1
findings.headline: New financial management system (ERPx) implementing enhanced controls; go-live targeted 16 November 2026.
findings.detail: The council is actively implementing Unit4 ERPx financial system with go-live date 16 November 2026. The system design includes formal journal authorisation processes, independent accrual transaction review/approval, Single Sign-On via Azure authentication, and multi-factor authentication for off-network users. Current manual controls remain in place until system go-live. This proactive remediation addresses multiple identified control weaknesses.
findings.matters: Lenders need confidence that management is actively remediating identified control gaps. The near-term system upgrade with specified enhanced controls demonstrates commitment to improving the control environment and reducing financial statement risk.
findings.figures: Go-live date: 16 November 2026.
findings.quote: The Council is currently implementing an upgraded financial system, with an anticipated go-live date of 16th November 2026. As part of the design of the controls within the new system, a journal authorisation process has been developed.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statemenet of Account 202526 Appendix 1
findings.headline: Multiple IT control deficiencies identified: excessive user access in Agresso, missing password policies in Logotech, absent Civica service agreement.
findings.detail: Three IT control deficiencies identified. Agresso: a new user was granted roles exceeding job requirements (subsequently removed). Logotech: no password configuration or lockout policies enforced, allowing weak user-defined passwords. Civica: service level agreement not obtained to verify controls operate appropriately. No evidence of unauthorized activity was found in audit testing, but these gaps increase risks of inappropriate access and data integrity compromise.
findings.matters: System access controls are preventive controls over financial data and transactions. Weak controls increase fraud and data manipulation risk. Lenders need assurance that financial systems and data have adequate safeguards.
findings.figures: No quantified impact; deficiencies identified across multiple systems.
findings.quote: During the audit, it was noted that for a sample Agresso new user within the audit period, the system roles granted to the new user exceeded those requested and required for the user's role.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statemenet of Account 202526 Appendix 1
findings.headline: No formal approval process for journal postings below £500k; capital journals above £500k lack documented audit trail.
findings.detail: Finance team members are effectively posting their own journals below £500k with only retrospective sampling-based monthly review. For capital journals above £500k, while senior staff approval is given, no documentation evidences this review. This is a recurring control weakness noted in the prior year audit and remains unresolved.
findings.matters: Formal approval and audit trails for journal entries are fundamental controls preventing unauthorized or erroneous transactions. The absence of these controls across a significant transaction volume increases fraud and error risk.
findings.figures: £500k threshold for approval requirement.
findings.quote: no formal approval process exists for those journals under £500k and assurance is taken from review of a sample of journals, below this threshold, on a monthly basis. There is a lack of audit trail for the review of capital journals which are above £500k.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statemenet of Account 202526 Appendix 1
findings.headline: Year-end accruals control error: £405,199 transposition variance with £2,037k extrapolated impact.
findings.detail: Testing of post-year-end payments and creditor completeness identified a £405,199 variance between an invoiced amount and the creditor raised at year end, resulting from human error in transposing information to the ledger. Although this specific transaction is immaterial, the extrapolated error for the population tested is £2,037k, indicating potential for significant liability misstatement if similar errors occur elsewhere.
findings.matters: Creditors completeness and accuracy is critical for lenders assessing liability disclosure. An extrapolated error of £2,037k is material to the financial statements (materiality threshold £9,980k), suggesting control gaps in year-end accrual procedures.
findings.figures: £405,199 variance identified; £2,037k extrapolated error.
findings.quote: the Audit Team identified a £405,199 variance between an invoiced amount and creditor raised at year end. This was the result of human error when transposing information from the client's calculations to the ledger.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statemenet of Account 202526 Appendix 1
findings.headline: Capital expenditure misclassification corrected: £1,041k reclassified between additions and REFCUS on Bath Riverside Project.
findings.detail: Auditor testing identified that capital expenditure on the Bath Riverside project (part-funded by council through Homes England but not creating a council-owned asset) had been incorrectly split between capital additions and Revenue Expenditure Financed by Capital under Statute (REFCUS). Recalculation using claim forms identified that capital additions had been understated by £1,041k. Management adjusted the financial statements to correct this.
findings.matters: A material adjustment on a major capital project raises questions about control robustness in capital accounting. This affects balance sheet reliability and suggests potential for similar errors in other projects.
findings.figures: £1,041k adjustment.
findings.quote: recalculation of the split identified that the figures disclosed in the financial statements are incorrect. We have recalculated the split and confirmed that additions have been understated by £1,041k and REFCUS similarly overstated by the same amount.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statemenet of Account 202526 Appendix 1
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit flagged as risk of significant weakness in financial sustainability for fourth consecutive audit year.
findings.detail: The auditors identify ongoing pressure from the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit as a risk of significant weakness relating to financial sustainability, consistent with findings in 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25. The council intends to apply for the High Needs Stability Grant / DSG Deficit Support Grant, which could write off up to 90% of the deficit subject to SEND reform plan approval, with the council funding the remaining 10%.
findings.matters: A four-year running audit finding on financial sustainability in a major service area signals structural imbalance rather than temporary pressure. Lenders need to understand whether the council can sustain services without ongoing grant support.
findings.figures: DSG deficit balance not quantified in this findings report.
findings.quote: Our risk assessment identified a risk of significant weakness in relation to financial sustainability, reflecting the ongoing pressure of the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit, consistent with our findings in 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: 13 Internal Audit Perfomance Update
findings.headline: Internal audit verified strong controls over Registration Services income following external auditor recommendation
findings.detail: Following a General Register Office external audit recommendation, the council conducted a review of Registration Services income governance and controls. The audit found a strong control environment across income collection, banking, certificate management, and payment processing, awarding Substantial Assurance (Level 4). Minor opportunities for enhancement were identified relating to banking discrepancy documentation and physical security procedures.
findings.matters: This confirms external audit concerns have been addressed and the service operates with effective financial controls and compliance with GRO requirements
findings.figures: Substantial Assurance opinion (Level 4) – the highest assurance level
findings.quote: The audit identified a strong control environment supporting the collection, recording and safeguarding of Registration Services income... A Substantial Assurance opinion (Level 4) has been awarded.

findings.paper_title: 13 Internal Audit Perfomance Update
findings.headline: Prior audit recommendations are mostly implemented, but five actions on Disabled Facilities Grants remain outstanding
findings.detail: Follow-up work on prior audit recommendations found all due recommendations implemented except for one audit report. Of nine Disabled Facilities Grants actions, four are complete but five remain in progress or outstanding. Children's OT team service redesign has paused some actions; Adults OT achieved a 74% reduction in open cases and 26% faster completion times, but joint risk register and formalised protocols remain unfinished.
findings.matters: Delays in implementing audit recommendations leave identified risks unaddressed and control gaps unresolved
findings.figures: 4 complete, 5 in progress or outstanding; 74% reduction in open DFG cases awaiting assessment; 26% reduction in time from referral to completion
findings.quote: During the completion of follow-ups between April and September 2026, it was found that all recommendations that were due had been implemented, with the exception of recommendations from one Internal Audit report that have not been fully implemented by the agreed due date.

findings.paper_title: 13 Internal Audit Perfomance Update
findings.headline: One audit found Limited Assurance (Level 2) on staff overpayment recovery controls
findings.detail: A debt management audit identified multiple governance and control weaknesses: the recovery framework is outdated, procedures are not fully documented, roles and responsibilities lack clarity, late payroll notifications contribute to overpayments, and manual processes create efficiency risks. The council accepted all findings and work is underway to implement remedial actions.
findings.matters: Internal control gaps in staff overpayment recovery indicate broader governance weaknesses that could affect financial risk management across the council
findings.figures: Limited Assurance (Level 2) – the lowest assurance level issued
findings.quote: one report has been issued to date where it was considered that the systems of internal control gave 'Limited Assurance' (Level 2). This Limited Assurance opinion related to a review of debt management, specifically around overpayments made to staff.

findings.paper_title: 9 Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statement of Accounts 202526
findings.headline: The council is managing a Dedicated Schools Grant deficit under a Department for Education Safety Valve Agreement, identified as a significant governance issue
findings.detail: The Annual Governance Statement records a DSG deficit being managed through a Safety Valve Agreement with the DfE, flagged alongside service demand and cost pressures as one of two significant governance issues requiring management action. Safety Valve Agreements are formal intervention arrangements triggered by unsustainable school deficits.
findings.matters: A Safety Valve Agreement signals that the council's schools funding has deteriorated sufficiently to trigger DfE intervention, restricting financial autonomy and indicating material budget stress in the schools sector
findings.figures: Not specified in this paper
findings.quote: The Annual Governance Statement records two 'significant' issues: A) Financial Challenge – Service Demand and Cost Pressures B) Children Services – Dedicated Schools Grant Deficit & the Safety Valve Agreement

findings.paper_title: 9 Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statement of Accounts 202526
findings.headline: Avon Pension Fund's funding level improved from 106% to 109% between the 2025 valuation and March 2026, moving employers out of deficit
findings.detail: The Fund's asset-to-liability ratio strengthened within a year, reducing accumulated deficits across member employers. The Fund holds £6.2bn in assets with £264.5m in highly liquid reserves and £2.0bn in listed equities, with 99.99% of contributions received on time.
findings.matters: Improved pension fund solvency reduces long-term contribution demands on employer councils, lowering future budget pressures and improving financial sustainability
findings.figures: Funding level: 106% (2025 valuation), 109% (March 2026); £6.2bn total assets; £264.5m liquid assets; £2.0bn listed equity; 99.99% on-time contribution receipt
findings.quote: The Funding level (i.e. the ratio of the Fund's assets to liabilities) was 106% at the last valuation in 2025. By March 2026 the funding level rose to 109%. The improved funding position has resulted in many employers moving out of a deficit position.

findings.paper_title: 9 Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statement of Accounts 202526
findings.headline: Grant Thornton has proposed an unmodified audit opinion on the council's 2025/26 financial statements
findings.detail: The audit is expected to conclude with a clean opinion on the council's financial statements. Adjustments made during the audit did not affect the total usable reserves.
findings.matters: An unmodified audit opinion confirms the financial statements fairly represent the council's financial position with no material issues or going concern risks
findings.figures: Unmodified opinion
findings.quote: Grant Thornton are currently proposing to issue an audit report including an unmodified audit opinion on the Council's 2025/26 Financial Statements.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statement of Accounts 202526 Appendix 8
findings.headline: Council's £46.5m Dedicated Schools Grant deficit, continuing from prior year, may force reserve drawdowns by 31 March 2028 if not resolved, risking medium-term financial sustainability.
findings.detail: The council has a £46.5m DSG deficit at March 2026, driven by Special Education Needs and Disabilities cost pressures. This is a continuing significant weakness from the prior year, and if not resolved by March 2028, the deficit may require funding from council reserves, which could reduce reserve levels to a point where medium-term financial sustainability is at risk. The council is working with the Department for Education on a management plan.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that the council will not face a forced drawdown of reserves that could undermine liquidity and financial stability. A £46.5m gap that consumes reserves represents material risk to the council's medium-term financial position.
findings.figures: £46.5m deficit at March 2026; deadline for resolution 31 March 2028
findings.quote: If the Council is not able to effectively reduce the residual DSG deficit and other accrued DSG deficits before 31 March 2028, these may need to be funded from the Council's own reserves. Reserve levels could reduce to a level putting the medium-term financial sustainability of the Council at risk.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & audited Statement of Accounts 202526 Appendix 2
findings.headline: Agresso system granted excessive user access during new user provisioning, identified and remediated post-audit
findings.detail: The audit found that for one new Agresso system user, the roles granted exceeded those requested and required for the role. Management identified and removed the inappropriate access post-audit review. The audit team confirmed this user did not post transactions to the Pension Fund ledger, but the issue indicates broader control weaknesses in IT user access provisioning.
findings.matters: Excessive system access granted during user provisioning increases risks of unauthorized data access, manipulation, or segregation of duties breaches. IT control failures create audit concern about the reliability of financial data and the ability to prevent fraud or errors in pension fund accounting.
findings.figures: One user affected; access subsequently removed
findings.quote: During the audit, it was noted that for a sample Agresso new user within the audit period, the system roles granted to the new user exceeded those requested and required for the user's role.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & audited Statement of Accounts 202526 Appendix 2
findings.headline: £400m reclassification of property investments from Level 3 to Level 2 reflects changing observability of valuations
findings.detail: Six property fund assets totalling £400,034k were reclassified from Level 3 (unobservable inputs) to Level 2 (observable inputs) due to updated confirmations from the funds. This reduced reported Level 3 investments from £1,576,690k to £1,176,656k and increased Level 2 from £4,304,680k to £4,704,714k. This affected disclosure only, not valuations.
findings.matters: Reclassification of £400m in assets between valuation hierarchies indicates the observability and reliability of investment valuations varies year to year, affecting how well the pension fund can track and defend its reported investment position to lenders and stakeholders.
findings.figures: £400,034k reclassified between Level 3 and Level 2
findings.quote: As a result of our challenge of the fair value hierarchy classification of investments, there were six assets held across two funds noted that were disclosed as Level 3, however upon review, it was apparent that a Level 2 classification was more appropriate.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & audited Statement of Accounts 202526 Appendix 2
findings.headline: £198m discrepancy in promised retirement benefits liability in draft accounts was a transposition error, now corrected
findings.detail: The draft pension fund accounts understated the promised retirement benefits liability by £198m. Note 1.28 in the draft disclosed £5,608m against the actual figure of £5,806m per the actuarial valuation. This was caused by a transposition error in accounts preparation and corrected in the final accounts.
findings.matters: A £198m error in pension liabilities, even if transcriptional, demonstrates the accounts required material quality control corrections and requires careful review by finance leaders and lenders assessing the council's true pension obligations and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Draft £5,608m vs actual £5,806m (£198m understatement)
findings.quote: The promised retirement benefits liability disclosed within Note 1.28 in the draft accounts is understated by £198m. Note 1.28 discloses a liability of £5,608m, whereas the corresponding disclosures in Notes 15 and 15a disclose a liability of £5,806m

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & audited Statement of Accounts 202526 Appendix 2
findings.headline: Brunel Pension Partnership wind-up and transfer to Local Pension Partnership Investment (LPPI) effective 1 April 2026 represents material change in fund governance
findings.detail: The pension fund transitioned from Brunel Pension Partnership to LPPI for investment management effective 1 April 2026. This altered investment administration, changed the audit query process requiring direct correspondence with individual fund managers instead of through Brunel, and created additional administrative burden on both the fund and auditors.
findings.matters: A material change in investment governance and pooling arrangements affects the council's control over pension asset management, administrative costs, and audit oversight of valuations. Lenders care about whether the council maintains robust oversight of its largest financial liability.
findings.figures: Transition effective 1 April 2026
findings.quote: The Fund transitioned from Brunel to LPPI with effect from 1 April 2026. Responsibility for the management of the Fund's pooled assets, including responding to audit queries, transferred to LPPI accordingly.

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & audited Statement of Accounts 202526 Appendix 2
findings.headline: £8.1m unadjusted misstatement in Level 3 pension fund investments remains in final accounts due to individually immaterial timing differences
findings.detail: The auditors identified cumulative timing and valuation differences totalling £8.142m between fund manager capital account statements and the pension fund's reported figures for Level 3 investments. While no single difference exceeded the audit reporting threshold, the aggregate variance was significant enough to report. The auditors determined adjustment was not required because differences were individually immaterial.
findings.matters: An £8m reported variance that remains unadjusted indicates ongoing challenges in the pension fund's investment valuation process and suggests the fund's balance sheet may contain other unreported differences of similar magnitude, affecting the reliability of the funding position.
findings.figures: £8.142m cumulative (£7.747m Non-Property, £0.396m Property Pooled Investment Vehicles)
findings.quote: We have identified a £8.1m unadjusted misstatements as at 31 March 2026 because of timing and valuation differences between Level 3 Investment fund manager capital account statements

findings.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & audited Statement of Accounts 202526 Appendix 2
findings.headline: £5.9m adjustment to pension fund assets for investment timing differences between fund managers and year-end reporting
findings.detail: The auditors identified a material adjustment relating to the 'Foresight Regional Investment VII LP' asset. The draft accounts reported £8.378m but the fund manager's capital account statement showed £14.310m. The difference arose because the final valuation was received after the Pension Fund's year-end reporting date, requiring correction in the final accounts.
findings.matters: Material adjustments to pension fund valuations indicate the council's investment reporting processes required audit correction and may signal ongoing challenges in reliably tracking pension liabilities, which significantly affect the council's balance sheet and ability to borrow.
findings.figures: £5.933m adjustment; draft figure £8.378m vs actual £14.310m
findings.quote: We identified several adjustments to the financial statements, one of which caused a £5.9m adjustment to the Pension Fund's Net Asset statement reported financial position

findings.committee: Corporate Policy Development and Scrutiny Panel
findings.paper_title: Children's Services Budget Report
findings.headline: The Quarter 1 2026/27 budget monitoring table gives risk-banded totals of £5.1m, £6.8m and £8.6m.
findings.detail: The table sets out Residential and Demand Budgets, Supporting at Home Costs and Staffing Pressures across low, mid-point and high-risk columns. The total row gives the three banded figures. The paper does not label the totals as an overspend.

findings.paper_title: Children's Services Financial Update Report
findings.headline: Residential care weekly unit costs at Bath & North East Somerset exceed regional comparators by over £1,000 and the England average by over £1,500
findings.detail: The council pays significantly more per placement than statistical neighbours or the England average. This is rooted in national structural factors: the South East has fewer children's homes than the North, forcing councils in this region to place children further from home, which increases costs and reduces availability of suitable local provision.
findings.matters: This is a structural cost disadvantage not driven by council inefficiency; it reflects the council's geographic position in a high-cost placement market, making it harder to manage demand pressures.
findings.figures: >£1,000 a week higher than regional comparators; >£1,500 higher than statistical neighbours and England average
findings.quote: B&NES is >£1,000 a week higher than regional comparators and >£1,500 higher than stat neighbours and the England average.

The quarter-on-quarter deterioration reflects crystallisation of ICB invoice write-offs and slippage in planned placement step-downs.
findings.matters: A £10.2m overspend in a core statutory service shows the council's spending significantly exceeded budget, and the fact that it worsened through the year indicates growing pressures that the council was unable to control or forecast.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Performance Report 2026_27 Q1
findings.headline: Strategic investments down £2.1m (21% loss) and protected from revenue impact only until 2029 by temporary statutory override
findings.detail: The council holds £10m in pooled strategic funds (£5m CCLA property, £3m FP Foresight infrastructure, £2m VT Gravis clean energy) now valued at £7.893m. Fair-value losses of £2.107m reflect that 'the value of equity, bonds and property have fallen significantly since the time of investment' due to 'high interest rates, weak growth, rising inflation and global uncertainty.' The losses are currently shielded from revenue by statutory override, but 'gains/losses will only be charged to revenue if/when the Council's holding in the pooled funds are sold, or from 2029/30 onwards when the override ends.'
findings.matters: A £2.1m unrealized loss signals that council investment returns will be below expectations; the statutory protection expires in 2029/30, at which point future losses could hit revenue unless sales or reserve support materializes
findings.figures: Historic cost: £10m; fair value 30 June 2026: £7.893m (loss £2.107m); CCLA at £4.208m (cost £5m), FP Foresight at £2.284m (cost £3m), VT Gravis at £1.401m (cost £2m); override expires 31 March 2029
findings.quote: In the current economic environment of high interest rates, weak growth, rising inflation and global uncertainty, the value of equity, bonds and property have fallen significantly since the time of investment.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Performance Report 2026_27 Q1
findings.headline: £10m in KBC Bank LOBO loans now variable at 4.50% with lender reset option every six months; refinancing risk if rates rise
findings.detail: The council holds two KBC LOBO loans (£5m each, maturing 2054) that have 'reached the end of their fixed interest period and have reverted to the variable rate of 4.50%. The lender has the option to change the interest rate at 6 monthly intervals.' If the lender exercises a reset, the borrower has the option to repay without penalty. The treasury adviser's economic review notes that market expectations have shifted to 'at least one rise in rates before the end of 2026,' creating near-term refinancing uncertainty.
findings.matters: £10m at variable rate with no interest-rate floor creates exposure to both higher costs and forced refinancing decisions at unfavourable times; the next reset opportunity is six months away
findings.figures: LOBO exposure: £10m (two loans); rate: 4.50% variable; maturity: 8 October 2054; interest reset: six-monthly at lender's option
findings.quote: All LOBO's have reached the end of their fixed interest period and have reverted to the variable rate of 4.50%. The lender has the option to change the interest rate at 6 monthly intervals. Should the lender use the option to change the rate, then at this point the borrower has the option to repay the loan without penalty.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Performance Report 2026_27 Q1
findings.headline: Council took £10m delayed borrowing specifically to maintain minimum £15m liquidity threshold; suggests structural cash shortfall
findings.detail: Of the £35m borrowed in Q1, the paper explicitly states £10m was 'delayed borrowing from 2025/26 to maintain the Council's liquidity indicator above £15.000m.' This is borrowing undertaken not to fund capital schemes but purely to meet working capital requirements. Minimum liquidity during the quarter hit £21.5m, suggesting only modest headroom above the £15m threshold.
findings.matters: Borrowing to maintain minimum cash balances indicates operations are not generating sufficient liquidity; this is a structural weakness that limits the council's ability to absorb shocks or accelerate spending
findings.figures: Delayed borrowing from prior year: £10m; minimum liquidity in quarter: £21.5m (date 29/06/2026); liquidity threshold: £15m
findings.quote: £10.000m of delayed borrowing from 2025/26 to maintain the Council's liquidity indicator above £15.000m, as well as £25.000m of borrowing to replace maturing loans.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Performance Report 2026_27 Q1
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement jumping 20% year-on-year to £464.6m while borrowing stays flat; council funding capital through reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The CFR forecast for 31 March 2027 is £464.627m versus actual £385.872m a year prior—a £78.755m increase. External borrowing stands at £295.772m, creating a £63.990m underborrowing position that the paper states is being managed by 're-investment of the internal balances including reserves, reducing the in-year borrowing costs in excess of the potential investment returns.' This strategy minimizes interest costs but depletes internal resources.
findings.matters: A 20% year-on-year CFR increase signals capital spending is accelerating; if funded by reserves rather than borrowing, reserve run-down becomes structural and limits the council's financial flexibility
findings.figures: CFR forecast 31 March 2027: £464.627m; CFR actual 31 March 2026: £385.872m (increase £78.755m); current borrowing: £295.772m; funding gap: £63.990m
findings.quote: The difference between the CFR of £385.872m and the Borrowing Portfolio of £295.772m represents re-investment of the internal balances including reserves, reducing the in-year borrowing costs in excess of the potential investment returns.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement of £386m substantially exceeds borrowing of £289m, with £97m gap filled by reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The council's underlying need to borrow (CFR) is £386m, but external borrowing stands at only £288.977m. The £97m gap is being bridged by re-investing internal reserves and cash balances, which yields lower returns than debt costs but depletes the council's financial buffer.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund capital rather than borrowing erodes the council's reserves and flexibility. Once reserves are exhausted, the council will need to borrow further or defer capital spending.
findings.figures: CFR £386m; borrowing £288.977m; reserve funding gap £97m
findings.quote: The difference between the CFR of £386m and the Borrowing Portfolio of £288.977m represents re-investment of the internal balances including reserves, reducing the in-year borrowing costs in excess of the potential investment returns.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Pension contribution prepayment consumed £20m of annual new borrowing
findings.detail: Of the £90m in new borrowing taken during the year, £20m was specifically drawn to fund an annual pension contribution prepayment. The remaining £70m replaced maturing loans. This represents a deliberate commitment to advance pension funding.
findings.matters: Pension prepayment decisions indicate forward cash planning but also represent a committed outflow that reduces borrowing capacity available for other capital or service needs.
findings.figures: £20m for pension prepayment; £70m to replace maturing debt; total new borrowing £90m
findings.quote: £20.000m of new loans taken out to cover the annual pension contribution prepayment and to maintain the Council's liquidity indicator above £15.000m

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital programme rephasing reduced debt repayment charges in the year
findings.detail: The council achieved a £2.087m underspend on interest and capital financing costs, with the Minimum Revenue Provision charge £0.181m below budget. This was attributable to delays in capital project delivery, signalling the council is not spending capital at the pace originally planned.
findings.matters: Capital programme delays indicate delivery risk and suggest planned capital spending may not materialise, which affects medium-term financial planning and service infrastructure investment.
findings.figures: MRP underspend £0.181m; total interest & capital financing variance £2.087m under budget
findings.quote: a lower Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) charge, reflecting the rephasing of capital projects

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Strategic investment portfolio showing £2.3m unrealised loss against purchase cost
findings.detail: The council holds £10m in strategic pooled funds now valued at £7.704m as at 31 March 2026. The CCLA property fund has fallen to £4.253m from £5m cost; FP Foresight infrastructure fund to £2.146m from £3m; VT Gravis clean energy fund to £1.304m from £2m. Losses are currently shielded from the revenue account by statutory override, but protection expires in 2029/30, at which point the council faces potential charges to revenue.
findings.matters: 23% capital loss on strategic holdings represents a deferred revenue pressure when the statutory override expires in 2029/30, or if the council needs to realise these investments earlier. This erodes financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Historic cost £10m; fair value £7.704m; CCLA £4.253m on £5m cost; Infrastructure fund £2.146m on £3m; Clean energy £1.304m on £2m
findings.quote: In the current economic environment of high interest rates, weak growth, rising inflation and global uncertainty, the value of equity, bonds and property have fallen significantly since the time of investment.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring, Cash Limits and Virements – 202627 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Heritage Services income under pressure from geopolitical factors, already £0.123m behind budget at May
findings.detail: Heritage Services (Roman Baths) achieved a net surplus of £11.738m in 2025/26 but fell £2.545m short of its rebased target due to lower visitor numbers. At end May 2026, admission income is already £0.123m (2.6%) behind budget. Geopolitical instability affecting Middle East transit, US inflation reducing visitor flows, and Asia-Pacific travel disruption are identified as material risks to forecast visitor numbers.
findings.matters: Heritage is a major revenue source (£11.7m+ net) but is highly exposed to external macro factors (geopolitics, currency, fuel costs) outside management control. The May shortfall suggests the risk is materialising early in the year. Q1 forecast is already showing real variance.
findings.figures: £11.738m net surplus 2025/26, £2.545m below target 2025/26, £0.123m (2.6%) behind budget May 2026, £0.000m-£0.750m forecast risk range
findings.quote: Heritage income figures are highly depended on tourist visitor numbers to the Roman Baths. With geo-political instability affecting inbound visitation, in particular from the US, due to inflation, and from Asia-Pacific, due to percentage of visitors who transit through Dubai / Doha, there is considerable risk to the budgeted visitor numbers for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring, Cash Limits and Virements – 202627 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Home to School Transport statutory service overspend recurring: £0.769m adverse in 2025/26, £0.4m-£0.8m risk in 2026/27
findings.detail: This statutory service overran by £0.769m in 2025/26 despite the budget being grown by £0.336m for inflation. Q1 forecasts continued risk of £0.4m-£0.8m as operator costs rise faster than assumed inflation and demand continues to grow. The council cannot refuse provision of this service but cannot control demand.
findings.matters: This is a statutory obligation with uncontrolled demand and supplier costs outpacing budget assumptions. The service is demonstrating a structural cost growth trend. The council must either find further budget or cut provision (not an option), making this a committed future pressure.
findings.figures: £0.769m adverse 2025/26 outturn, £0.336m inflation growth in 2026/27 budget, £0.400m-£0.800m forecast risk 2026/27
findings.quote: Home to School Transport ended 2025/26 with a £0.769m adverse outturn position... The need to respond to continued increases in demand for Home to School Transport, alongside operator cost pressures exceeding assumed inflation, presents an ongoing risk to the budgetary position currently estimated between £0.400m and £0.800m.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring, Cash Limits and Virements – 202627 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit reached £46.505m, additional overspend anticipated for 2026/27, funding dependent on DfE SEND plan approval
findings.detail: DSG overspent by £13.716m in 2025/26, taking the cumulative deficit to £46.505m (ringfenced from general fund but material governance issue). Additional overspend for 2026/27 is anticipated driven by SEND costs. The council submitted its SEND Reform Plan to the DfE on 19 June 2026 (deadline date) and is awaiting approval for the High Needs Stability Grant, which would provide mitigation.
findings.matters: While ringfenced, a £46.5m cumulative deficit is material and growing. The SEND overspend is driving this growth. Funding mitigation depends on external approval that is not yet secured. The council has no control over the approval timeline or outcome.
findings.figures: £13.716m overspend 2025/26, £46.505m cumulative deficit at 31/03/2026, SEND Reform Plan submitted 19 June 2026
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) overspent by £13.716m for 2025/26 taking the cumulative to deficit at the end of 2025/26 to £46.505m... Additional overspend for 2026/27 is anticipated at a higher level.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring, Cash Limits and Virements – 202627 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Commercial Income Risk Reserve being rapidly depleted from £3.94m to £0.84m, limiting buffer for income volatility
findings.detail: The reserve created to weather commercial income fluctuations is being drawn down by £2.4m to mitigate pressures in Commercial Estate, Bath Quays South, and the Housing Delivery Company (Aequus). This reduces the reserve from £3.942m to £0.840m, leaving minimal headroom. Further income deterioration would rapidly exhaust this buffer.
findings.matters: Reserves are the council's shock absorber for income volatility. A buffer of £0.84m on a £117m capital programme and council-wide commercial operations is minimal. Depletion signals the council is moving into a less defensible financial position.
findings.figures: Opening balance £3.942m, planned draw £2.400m, residual balance £0.840m
findings.quote: The available balance on the reserve brought forward from 2025/26 is £3.942m. The Quarter 1 forecast assumes that £2.400m of this reserve will be required to mitigate against the overall forecast position, based on taking the mid-point range of risk forecast for those income streams reported above, which would reduce this reserve to £0.840m.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring, Cash Limits and Virements – 202627 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Commercial asset portfolio materially underperforming: Bath Quays South and Commercial Estate combining for £1.1m-£1.65m forecast risk
findings.detail: Bath Quays South offices were £0.665m adverse in 2025/26; Commercial Estate was £0.511m adverse. Both are forecast to continue underperforming in 2026/27 with combined risk of £1.1m-£1.65m. Rental income shortfalls are the key driver, with properties held void while being marketed. The council is also paying increased borrowing costs to support these underperforming assets.
findings.matters: These are balance-sheet assets supposed to generate council revenue. Persistent underperformance raises concerns about asset quality, management effectiveness, and the affordability of the borrowing that finances them. The void holdings also represent stranded capital.
findings.figures: £0.665m Bath Quays adverse 2025/26, £0.511m Commercial Estate adverse 2025/26, £1.100m-£1.650m combined forecast risk
findings.quote: The Commercial Estate ended 2025/26 £0.511m over budget and this adverse position is currently considered likely to continue into 2026/27. The Bath Quays South Office rental income target...ended 2025/26 with an adverse budget position of £0.665m... the current forecast is a material budget pressure of £1.100m - £1.650m.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring, Cash Limits and Virements – 202627 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Children's Services structural overspend recurring: £10.2m actual loss in 2025/26, £5.4m-£8.9m forecast for 2026/27
findings.detail: Children's Services overran by £10.182m in 2025/26 driven by residential placement demand and care cost pressures. Q1 2026/27 forecasts another £5.35m-£8.9m overspend despite growth allocation and a focused transformation programme. The council has established a placements taskforce and is engaging with regional networks, but uncontrolled demand continues to outpace budget.
findings.matters: This is the single largest identified budget risk and is recurring across consecutive years. It represents uncontrolled demand pressure in a statutory service directly affecting council financial standing. Even the best-case forecast (£5.35m) is material.
findings.figures: £10.182m overspend 2025/26, £5.350m-£8.900m forecast 2026/27, residential placements 155 (May 2026) vs 143 (May 2025)
findings.quote: Children's Services closed the 2025/26 financial year with a £10.182m overspend, largely driven by continued demand and residential placement costs... a significant material forecast of £5.350m - £8.900m over budget is currently being projected.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring, Cash Limits and Virements – 202627 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Council forecasts £5.32m Q1 adverse variance, requiring full contingency and reserve depletion
findings.detail: The Q1 forecast shows an adverse net variance of £5.32m, mitigated by using the full £2.68m corporate contingency and a £2.4m draw from the Commercial Income Risk Reserve. Directorates have been tasked with developing recovery plans by Q2, but the underlying risk across the organisation remains high. This leaves minimal headroom for further pressures.
findings.matters: The council is relying on full use of contingency at Q1, when typically headroom should extend further into the year. If recovery plans don't materialise and reserves are depleted, the council loses financial flexibility and may struggle to absorb unexpected pressures.
findings.figures: £5.320m adverse variance, £2.680m corporate contingency (fully used), £2.400m Commercial Income Risk Reserve draw
findings.quote: The forecast position of the Council's 2026/27 Revenue Budget as at the end of Quarter 1 (June 2026) is an adverse net variance of £5.320m mitigated by Corporate Contingency Release & Commercial Income Risk Reserve Utilisation.

findings.paper_title: E3653 Appendix 5 - Revenue Savings Monitor
findings.headline: Regeneration services unable to achieve savings targets due to grant income dependency and cost recovery constraints
findings.detail: The Regeneration service reports that both new and existing savings targets are challenging to meet because the service is heavily dependent on grant income already bid for and has very limited ability to recover additional costs elsewhere.
findings.matters: When services depend on external grant funding to meet savings targets, the council loses control over achieving its budget plan if grants are not awarded or are withdrawn; this signals structural vulnerability in budget delivery
findings.figures: £50k variance on new regeneration income (partially mitigated by one-off income)
findings.quote: Both new and historic savings targets are challenging to meet. The service is highly dependant upon grant income which has already been bid for with very limited opportunities to recover extra costs.

findings.paper_title: E3653 Appendix 5 - Revenue Savings Monitor
findings.headline: Multiple property and commercial income targets not materialising; three separate delays totalling £625k
findings.detail: Commercial property income is £200k short due to underperformance between commercial and corporate portfolios. Corporate Estate disposal savings of £275k have not materialised because identified properties have minimal impact on running costs. Bath Quays South office building has £150k delayed income target due to partial vacancy; full occupancy not expected until May 2026.
findings.matters: Persistent property and commercial income shortfalls across multiple parts of the portfolio suggest the council's asset strategy is not generating expected returns, indicating either occupancy challenges or slower lease-up than planned
findings.figures: Commercial Estate £200k shortfall; Corporate Estate £275k delay; Bath Quays South £150k delay
findings.quote: A shortfall in income target between the Commercial and Corporate Estates has led to a delay in achieving this savings target.

findings.paper_title: E3653 Appendix 5 - Revenue Savings Monitor
findings.headline: Roman Baths visitor income continues below budget; £2.454m adverse variance in 2025/26, rebased for 2026/27
findings.detail: Visitor numbers to the Roman Baths remain below the 1.1m budgeted target, preventing the service from achieving its budgeted surplus. The 2025/26 outturn shows an adverse variance of £2.454m. The council has rebased 2026/27 income targets downward in a revised business plan, treating this as permanent income loss rather than temporary underperformance.
findings.matters: Structural erosion of income from a major council asset suggests either the visitor market has changed or the original business case was optimistic; the council is now absorbing this as ongoing budget pressure
findings.figures: £2.454m adverse outturn 2025/26; 1.1m visitor target; £2.148m ongoing budget pressure
findings.quote: As a result of a continuation of visitor numbers below the budgeted 1.1m at the Roman Baths, the Service has not achieved the budgeted surplus. The 25/26 Outturn position is an adverse £2.454m.

findings.paper_title: E3653 Appendix 5 - Revenue Savings Monitor
findings.headline: £2m staffing restructuring saving from Being Our Best programme not delivered; execution delayed
findings.detail: The council budgeted for £2.5m of staffing savings from the Being Our Best organisational restructuring in 2024/25 plus a further £2m in 2025/26. Delays to the programme mean it will only partially deliver, with the full £2m 2025/26 savings now not achieved. This cascades into delays to service restructuring proposals.
findings.matters: A major staffing restructuring falling short by £2m signals execution risk on a core efficiency plan the council built its budget around; this represents ongoing structural cost pressure that will need to be addressed
findings.figures: £2m variance; £2.5m 2024/25 target plus £2m 2025/26 target
findings.quote: The programme will partially deliver against the £2.5m built into the budget for 2024/25, but will not deliver the additional £2m in the 2025/26 budget

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Cabinet Report 25-26
findings.headline: Collection Fund adverse variance of £0.240m worse than estimated; Council Tax deficit of £0.562m created unexpected pressure
findings.detail: The outturn Collection Fund position was £0.240m worse than the provision made in the 2026/27 budget. Council Tax in particular was adversely affected by lower second homes and long-term empty properties, student occupied property increases, and bad debt write-offs, creating a £0.562m deficit of which the council's share was £0.218m. The total council share of the Collection Fund deficit increased by £0.396m from budget estimate.
findings.matters: Income forecasting accuracy is deteriorating, and the council is facing recurring council tax collection issues (bad debt, property classification changes) that suggest underlying collection risk.
findings.figures: £0.240m total variance worse than estimated; £0.562m Council Tax deficit; £0.218m council share; £0.396m worse than budget estimate; £1.724m Business Rates deficit (council share)
findings.quote: The non LCTS elements of the Collection Fund ended the year in an adverse position, with a deficit of £0.935m mainly due to less than budgeted second homes and long-term empty properties where a premium is charged, an increase in student occupied properties and a higher than forecast increase in the bad debt provision.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Cabinet Report 25-26
findings.headline: General Fund un-earmarked reserve sits at £12.584m, within but tight to the £12.0m–£13.2m risk range
findings.detail: The uncommitted non-earmarked reserve of £12.584m is within the budget risk assessment range set for 2026/27 (£12.0m–£13.2m), but there is minimal headroom. Further deterioration would breach the lower bound and require reserves to be rebuilt in future years.
findings.matters: The council has limited headroom for unforeseen shocks or if the structural pressures (children's services, SEND) continue to worsen. Any further reserve drawdown would leave the council below its minimum comfort level.
findings.figures: £12.584m actual; £12.0m–£13.2m target range
findings.quote: The year-end position of uncommitted non-earmarked reserves was £12.584m. The 2026/27 budget risk assessment, contained within the Budget and Council Tax 2026/27 and Financial Outlook Report to Council on 24th February 2026 set a range of between £12.0m and £13.2m to meet those risks.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Cabinet Report 25-26
findings.headline: Home to School Transport continues to pressure budget with rising SEN demand costs
findings.detail: Home to School Transport presented a £0.769m adverse variance in 2025/26 driven by increased demand, particularly increased Special Educational Needs (SEN) demand. This follows the broader pattern of SEND cost inflation across the council and suggests ongoing structural pressure in this service.
findings.matters: SEN-related cost pressures are appearing across multiple budget lines (residential placements, SEND transport, education staffing), indicating a systemic driver rather than isolated variances.
findings.figures: £0.769m adverse variance; driven by SEN demand increases
findings.quote: Home to School Transport continues to present financial pressure with increased demand, and in particular, increased Special Educational Needs (SEN) demand, resulting in an adverse variance for the service of £0.769m.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Cabinet Report 25-26
findings.headline: Commercial income underperformance: Heritage Services visitor numbers fell short of aggressive budget; Bath Quays South rental delays persist
findings.detail: Heritage Services set an aggressive income target for 2025/26 but visitor numbers fell below budget, particularly during peak pricing periods, creating a £2.454m adverse variance. Combined with one-off restructuring costs, the service outturn was significantly adverse. Bath Quays South floor space rental was delayed, and delays in implementing the corporate landlord model and estate rationalisation contributed a £1.593m variance across Commercial Estate and Regeneration.
findings.matters: Income from heritage and commercial property is not materialising as forecast, suggesting either the budget assumptions were unrealistic or demand drivers have shifted. The ongoing delays in Bath Quays South suggest these are not one-off issues.
findings.figures: £2.454m Heritage Services adverse variance; £1.593m Commercial Estate/Regeneration variance from Bath Quays South delays
findings.quote: An aggressive income target was set for Heritage Services for 2025/26, but unfortunately visitor numbers were lower than budgeted, with larger visitor shortfalls crucially happening during months with peak pricing periods.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Cabinet Report 25-26
findings.headline: Revenue Budget Contingency Reserve drawn by £1.455m; Commercial Income Risk Reserve drawn by £1.176m to cover the outturn
findings.detail: The £2.631m revenue overspend is entirely funded by earmarked reserves rather than managed within budget. The Revenue Budget Contingency was drawn by £1.455m (of which £0.840m was one-off invoices written off), and the Commercial Income Risk Reserve by £1.176m for Commercial Estate (£0.511m) and Bath Quays South (£0.665m) rental income shortfalls. The Commercial Income Risk Reserve was itself created only recently by repurposing reserves and transferring £3.500m from the Business Rates Reserve.
findings.matters: The council is funding operational overspends from reserves created for risk mitigation, not from operational income. This is unsustainable if the underlying drivers (demand, income shortfalls) are structural rather than cyclical.
findings.figures: £2.631m overall revenue overspend; £1.455m from Revenue Budget Contingency; £1.176m from Commercial Income Risk Reserve; Commercial Estate pressure £0.511m; Bath Quays South pressure £0.665m
findings.quote: It is proposed that the £2.631m adverse variance is funded by the following drawdowns from Earmarked Reserves: £1.176m from the Commercial Income Risk Reserve to fund the associated adverse variances within Commercial Estate (£0.511m) and Regeneration (£0.665m).

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Cabinet Report 25-26
findings.headline: Being Our Best Programme delivered only 65% of £14.012m savings target; £2.479m undelivered in-year
findings.detail: Of approved savings proposals totalling £14.012m, 65% (£9.149m) were delivered in full, 15% (£2.040m) were mitigated through contingency elsewhere, and 20% (£2.823m) were delayed into 2026/27. The Pay & Grading Review resulted in a net increase in salary costs of £1.721m, exceeding budget and creating both an in-year and ongoing pressure. The residual £2.209m savings target was carried forward into 2026/27.
findings.matters: Savings programmes are not delivering as planned, and compensation from elsewhere masks underperformance. A pay award has added £1.721m recurring pressure with no offsetting efficiency gain, eroding the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £14.012m total savings target; £9.149m (65%) delivered; £2.823m (20%) delayed; £2.479m in-year shortfall; £2.209m carried forward to 2026/27; £1.721m Pay & Grading overspend
findings.quote: The Savings target relating to the Being our Best Programme in 2025/26 of £2.479m has not been delivered in year.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Cabinet Report 25-26
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant accumulated deficit of £46.505m, with £13.716m added in-year from SEND cost inflation
findings.detail: The centrally held DSG elements overspent by £13.716m due to significant increases in numbers and cost of SEND placements, carried forward with a brought-forward deficit of £32.789m. While the government will provide a High Needs Stability Grant of £41.931m, the council will face a residual £4.573m gap from 2028/29 when the statutory override ends. The DFE has recognised councils will continue to generate deficits until it takes over the High Needs Block in April 2028.
findings.matters: SEND cost inflation is outpacing funding growth. Although ringfenced from the general fund, it signals acute market pressures (placement sufficiency, care complexity, staff inflation) that are hitting the council's controllable services simultaneously.
findings.figures: £46.505m total DSG overspend; £13.716m in-year addition; £32.789m brought forward; £41.931m High Needs Stability Grant; £4.573m residual gap from 2028/29
findings.quote: The centrally held elements of the DSG were over budget by £13.716m, due to significant increases in numbers and cost of placements for children with SEND, which is funded from the High Needs Block within the DSG.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Cabinet Report 25-26
findings.headline: Children's Services £10.182m overspend driven by £8.107m residential placements pressure, with £1.510m arising in Q4 2025/26
findings.detail: The council closed 2024/25 with a £4.775m overspend in children's services, and despite additional budget provision in 2025/26, the situation worsened. Eight residential placements added in Q4 2024/25 created a recurring £2.700m pressure, compounded by a further £4.567m from additional placements in 2025/26. Of the £8.107m total residential placements overspend, £1.510m arose in Q4 alone, driven by escalation from lower-cost support and the increasing complexity of need requiring higher-cost packages.
findings.matters: This represents a structural demand crisis that is growing year-on-year. The recurring nature of Q4 placement increases and the market-driven cost inflation indicate this is unlikely to be a one-off issue, and the council's own transformation programme may not resolve it at the pace overspending is occurring.
findings.figures: £10.182m overspend; £8.107m residential placements pressure; £4.567m additional placements in 2025/26; £1.510m Q4 2025/26 placements; £2.700m recurring from Q4 2024/25 placements
findings.quote: Of the total residential placements pressure of £8.107m, £1.510m arose in quarter 4 of 2025/26 due to additional placements and revised care planning assumptions.

findings.paper_title: Budget & Council Tax 2026-27 and Financial Outlook
findings.headline: Un-earmarked reserves are at lower end of risk-assessed range (£12.58m vs required £12.0-13.2m), providing limited headroom for unforeseen events
findings.detail: The council's General Fund un-earmarked reserve of £12.58m sits within the risk-assessed range of £12.0-13.2m but represents only 6.5% of Net Budget Requirement. The S151 Officer judges this 'adequate', but it provides minimal buffer. Given the £1.66m Q3 overspend forecast and £2.62m contingency held within the budget, the reserve is constrained.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand financial resilience. Lower reserves reduce flexibility to handle unexpected shocks, economic downturns, or service demand spikes. The council is operating at the minimum safe level.
findings.figures: Un-earmarked reserves £12.58m; risk-assessed range £12.0-13.2m; represents 6.5% of Net Budget Requirement (£193.17m)
findings.quote: The budget risk assessment has set a range of between £12.0m and £13.2m to meet those risks. The available balance is £12.58m which is within the budget risk assessment range and represents 6.5% of the Net Budget Requirement. I consider this to be an adequate working balance.

findings.paper_title: Budget & Council Tax 2026-27 and Financial Outlook
